whisper_segs.text: Good morning, it's seven o'clock on Wednesday, the 25th of February.
This is Morning Ireland with Gavin Jennings and Justin McCarthy.
Today, a turnaround for the ages, Trump's long State of the Union address, the Midwest
says no to taking water from the Shannon to Dublin.
Also, still no drugs tests for Gardaí, a plan to save GPs and the 70-year-old Dublin
woman rowing in a world championship.
In business, fuel prices rise marginally and new rental rules.
What changes for tenants and landlords on Sunday?
In sport, the West's awake.
Galway's Alex Murphy makes Champions League debut as Newcastle progress to the last 16
while Bodo's Blitz leaves Inter in the cold.
Good morning, stay with us, we're with you till nine o'clock on RTÉ Radio 1 online and
on the RTÉ News Channel.
The news is read now by Ailish Shihy.
In the United States, President Donald Trump has delivered his State of the Union speech
in which he defended his tariff policy and insisted he will push ahead with imposing
tariffs despite last week's Supreme Court ruling.
He also signalled a further clampdown on illegal immigrants in the US.
Our Washington correspondent Sean Whelan.
President Trump refrained from the ill-tempered attack on the Supreme Court he made last week,
simply calling the decision unfortunate.
He insisted the ruling clarified his powers to impose tariffs without congressional approval
and said most countries and companies want to stick with the agreements already made
for fear the president might impose higher levels.
He launched what he called a war on fraud, claiming there was rampant welfare fraud in
state budgets, implying much of it was carried out by migrants from third world countries
like Somalia, which provoked angry outbursts from Minnesota representative Ilhan Omar,
who is of Somali origin.
The anti-fraud drive will be led by Vice President J.D. Vance.
President Trump insisted he wants to find a diplomatic solution with Iran, but was adamant
the Iranians will not get nuclear weapons.
He also introduced numerous guests during the speech, including war heroes, victims
of crime and the Olympic gold medal winning USA ice hockey team.
Sean Whelan, RTE News, Washington.
Objections have been lodged against plans by Ishqa Airin for a Shannon pipeline.
The utility applied in December for planning permission for the pipeline, which it wants
to extract over 300 million litres of water a day from the River Shannon.
The objections have been lodged by communities in the Midwest because of environmental concerns.
Our Midwest correspondent, Petula Martin.
Ishqa Airin proposes constructing a 170 kilometre steel pipeline to pump drinking water from
the River Shannon at the Parteen Basin to the greater Dublin region.
The pipeline is a critical infrastructure project, it says, which would provide a secure
water supply with capacity to address the needs of up to 50% of the population.
Consultation on the plan closes to the public today, and objections have been lodged by
groups across the Midwest who oppose it.
The River Shannon Protection Alliance says the project is not necessary, will damage
water flows to Limerick and cause major ecological damage to Loch Derg and the River Shannon.
It says Ishqa Airin has not explored other water sources.
Authorities in Clare and Tipperary have written in opposition to the project, and Limerick
City and County Council is holding a special meeting next week to decide if it will make
a submission.
The Taoiseach Michal Martin will formally apologise to survivors of institutional abuse
in the Dáil later today.
It follows a hunger strike by four survivors of abuse in industrial and reformatory schools
that lasted for over 50 days outside Leinster House last year.
They had called for Health Amendment Act cards and access to a state contributory pension
in recognition of the lasting impact of the abuse they endured as children.
The government has since agreed a package of additional supports, including measures
covering health, education, housing and funeral costs.
The Special Advocate for Survivors has welcomed the move.
A case by a Belfast journalist who says he has been the target of systematic monitoring
by the UK state, begins a legal case against the PSNI and the security services in London today.
Vincent Kearney is the Northern Editor of RTE News.
Here's our Northern Correspondent, Conor McCauley.
Before he joined RTE and became its Northern Editor, Vincent Kearney had a long career
with the BBC in Belfast.
He worked as its Home Affairs Correspondent, a role that saw him focus on security and policing.
It emerged that MI5, the British security service, had been accessing his phone data,
so he took a legal case to try and establish the scale of the monitoring.
That case begins today in London, but Mr Kearney says pre-hearing disclosure shows that the
PSNI, MI5 and others engaged in systematic monitoring of him over many years, in an attempt
to establish his sources for certain stories.
Kearney's case is being backed by his former employers, the BBC.
It's due to run for several days at a special tribunal that deals with breaches of rules
around covert intelligence gathering.
Some of it will be heard in public, but some will be dealt with in closed hearings.
Conor McCauley, RTE News, Belfast.
And now the weather.

Ronan Kelly.
Thanks, Justin.
If it wasn't for the young women out in DCU, the papers would be a very grim read this
morning.
There are so many downbeat stories and so many people complaining.
Michael McDool is giving out about dead drummers, Paul Murphy is giving out about Google pizzas
and everyone's giving out about Sinn Féin.
The young women at DCU Helix are the contestants in the National Junk Couture competition where
they make dresses from waste material.
Gone are the days of tinfoil skirts and bin bag bodices.
To go by the pictures in this morning's papers, these are now spectacular creations, professionally
made.
Those photos from the competition are in the Times, Independent and Mail, while the examiner
front page has a large picture of one of the creations from a community college in Roscommon.
It has a maritime theme and is made of sardine tins, rope netting and shells with a train
of what looks like dead fish.
The examiner lead story beside that photo is also marine related.
It's a report on a new maritime security strategy.
This, the paper says, will allow the Navy to board and inspect Russian shadow vessels
travelling through Irish waters.
And big tech is preoccupying the papers this morning.
The Irish Daily Mail tells us that yesterday the Data Protection Commissioner told the
Oireachtas Committee on AI that his office is up against very well-resourced legal teams
when it comes to fining social media companies.
Although the Independent reports he denied that his team treats big tech companies with
kid gloves and said they've already levied fines of 4 billion euro.
Representatives of Google were also before the committee and TD Paul Murphy pointed out
to them that their AI tool is giving false answers, like saying you can use glue to stick
cheese to pizza.
Google said those kinds of results are very rare and when they see them, they change them.
Michael McDool is not going to like that last bit about pizzas.
He's complaining in his column in the Times about media editors focusing on what he believes
are irrelevant stories.
For example, he says the death of a drummer in a band that was big 20 years ago.
Most people, he said, wouldn't be able to answer his name in a quiz.
And don't get him started on curling.
He said he was left bored by seeing it in the Olympics and he thinks the idea that countries
subsidising it with millions is a big waste of money.
Back to serious politics and despite the fact that Fianna Fáil is celebrating 100 years,
it's Sinn Féin that's getting most column inches in the papers today.

their electricity than homeowners do.

euro loan for Ukraine.

is not good.
not the way to resolve this conflict. Mary Lou herself is in the mail with an opinion piece
criticising the government for forcing through student housing in Cabra when nearby TU Dublin
already has plans for such housing. And Mary Lou is being criticised by unionists in the Belfast
Telegraph. She posted a tribute to Brendan Bick Macfarlane on the first anniversary of his death.
She said he had a life well lived. The paper notes that Brendan Macfarlane was convicted of being
part of an attack on a bar in Belfast that left five dead and 60 injured. And the last bit of
giving out. Fiona Looney in her column in the mail quotes Louis Walsh's bitter word for Simon Cowell.
He'd heard that Simon Cowell has a new boy band. It's called December the 10th,
after the date it was formed. December the 10th, says Louis Walsh, it should be called April the
1st. Ronan Kelly, ten past seven. We'll hear some of Donald Trump's one hour, 50 minutes
State of the Union address later, but up next we'll be talking about drugs tests for Gardaí.
Morning Ireland, 12 minutes past seven. Drug testing for serving Gardaí, promised five years
ago after a major report into Garda corruption six years ago, and still not in place. Highlighted
by the Policing and Community Safety Authority, formerly the Policing Authority and the Garda
Inspectorate. They've just published their review of the recommendations that they made in that
report countering the threat of internal corruption and their chairperson Elaine Byrne is with us now.
Elaine Byrne, good morning and thank you for taking our call today. Can you remind us first
about that 2020 report, why it was carried out and what it found? Yes, the 2020 report
countering the threat of internal corruption looked at behaviours in on Garda Síochána,
the backdrop of various convictions and suspensions and concern in the public around
behaviours of members of staff and of on Garda Síochána. There were in all some 34 recommendations
and six years on the report has found that 13 of those have been implemented and six partially
implemented and 14, as you've outlined there, including drugs testing and internal vetting,
have not been implemented. So just over half implemented in full or in part and you've
highlighted drug tests, why? Well, you know, guards carry firearms, they drive at high speed,
they make critical decisions under pressure and if a member of on Garda Síochána is under the
impairment by drugs, reaction times can drop, judgment is affected and indeed the use of force
potentially is unsafe and roads policing can become dangerous. Drug use can create risks
in terms of the integrity of evidence, mishandling, vulnerabilities, blackmail
and links to criminal networks. Yes, but in March 2021, Elaine, a Garda inspected report
on tackling Garda corruption found the use of illegal drugs among the workforce
quote was acknowledged as a serious concern but do we know if it's extensive?
I would say that in my conversations with senior leadership in the guards across the country
that there is a deep concern about the use of drug taking by a minority of members and staff
and that is borne out by various convictions that we've seen come through the courts
in terms of drug related offences, possession of controlled substances and supplying drugs.
You know, also there have been convictions and there are ongoing investigations into
members accepting bribes, assisting criminal organisations and misusing confidential public
databases but you know on Garda Síochána there's almost 19,000 staff and members and
they're representative of the Irish public and as with the Irish public there are elements who
use drugs and the Gardaí are no different. Testing was due to be introduced before the
end of 2021. Laws were passed in 2024. In a statement from the Department of Justice to us
last night they said the minister's officials are working closely with Garda Síochána and
with drafters within the office of the Attorney General to finalise the regulations which will
underpin this. They say the regulations are complex and will require thorough consideration
but are now at an advanced stage of drafting. Although I note that in a statement to the
Irish Times last year they also said that officials were working with Garda Síochána
and drafters within the office of the AG to finalise the regulations that would underpin
the rollout of drug testing. Regulations are complex, will require thorough consideration,
remain subject to legal advice but it's hoped they will be in place before the end of the year.
Nothing's changed. What's the delay in your view? Look, the guards have undergone a significant
period of reform with the introduction of the new act, the Policing and Community Safety
Act and within that there's been a whole series of regulations on the behaviours of guards.
I don't believe this is something that the Garda leadership or indeed the minister
is opposed to. I think the pace of it is something that concerns the authority and
it's something we'll be discussing on Thursday at our public meeting with the leadership of Garda
Síochána but it is disappointing. Drug testing is not a controversial initiative, it is something
that's used throughout many other police jurisdictions and indeed in many areas of
employment life if you're a truck driver and so forth but we would hope that the department
would introduce this as they've indicated before the end of the year.
Internal vetting you raised too. Vetting of what and for what?
Well vetting of Garda members and vetting of Garda staff and the purpose of Garda vetting,
like drug testing, it's not controversial, it's used in many other jurisdictions.
It checks the background, the conduct, the financial situation and associations of people.
While they're guarding because it is done when they're joining the force, yes?
Yeah exactly, it's done when they enter Temple more but people's lives change, you know,
after 5, 10, 20 years service, the new relationships, financial problems can arise,
people can engage in substance abuse, their lifestyle changes and ultimately guards have
access to sensitive databases, criminal intelligence, evidence and informants
and vetting can help at an early stage and detect links to organised crime,
undisclosed relationships and debts that individuals may have. So it's a proactive
step in protecting Garda members. Is it not being done?
It's not after Temple more, no. So once you leave Temple more, once your term as a recruit is over
you're done and dusted. So the purpose of this step will be that it will be periodic
internal vetting of Garda staff and members throughout their career. So instead of waiting
for an incident to occur, which requires reactive steps and investigations and what have you,
this will be a proactive step in helping the Garda members and the public.
And why has it to be done?
Well, it's a cultural change that is something that I think, like the drug testing, it's something
that is new to the organisation. But again, I, you know, the Garda leadership team and our
conversations with them are positively disposed to it and it is something, again, we're discussing
at our public meeting on Thursday with the guards. But, you know, like tone comes from the top in
terms of culture, but culture ultimately lives in middle. And so I think internal vetting is
important to help people like sergeants and inspectors and supervisors shape the everyday
experience of members. Elaine Byrne, Chairperson of the Policing and Community Safety Authority.
Thank you very much for speaking with us this morning. Almost 20 past seven.
Objections to plans by Aisheke Arron to extract over 300 million litres of water a day from the
River Shannon to boost supplies in Dublin and the east of the country have been lodged by
communities in the Midwest who are opposed to the project. Aisheke Arron applied for planning
permission for the pipeline in December. Campaign groups who object to the project have raised
environmental concerns. Our Midwest correspondent Petula Martin joins us now. Petula, at the EPA,
the Environmental Protection Agency, has warned of potential water shortages in Dublin during the
summer months due to rising demand. What is Aisheke Arron proposing? Yes, Justin, it doesn't
feel like there could be a water shortage in any part of the country following recent weeks of
rainfall. But with a growing population and demand for housing, Dublin faces a severe water shortage
if a resolution isn't found. Aisheke Arron's proposal is to build a steel pipeline that will
pump drinking water from the River Shannon at the Parteen Basin just below Lough Derg, bringing it
to the east of the country. It will be just over 170 kilometres in length and it says it will have
capacity to support the water supply needs of up to 50% of the population, including 1.7 million
people in the greater Dublin area and another 800,000 people in towns in the Midlands and east
of the country. Aisheke Arron says this is a once in a generation project and the pipeline is a critical
piece of infrastructure. And not everyone supports that pipeline, Petula. What is the reason for the
objections that have been lodged? Well, one of the main groups opposed to the plan is the River
Shannon Protection Alliance and it says the pipeline will damage water flows to Limerick and cause major...
ecological damage to Loch Derg and the River Shannon. It says the project is not
necessary and that alternative water sources have not been explored properly
by Ishqa Éireann and it points to groundwater in Kildare and Meath and the
reservoir in Paola Fuca and the group says Limerick's water supply is already
under strain and its waste water treatment needs a substantial upgrade. It
says the project if it gets planning it will cut the water flow to Limerick in
summer months. When water is needed in the Greater Dublin area during the
summer it's also needed in the Shannon and this can be seen when the ESB
closes the turbines at Ardna Crossia power plant during the summer to keep
the old course of the river alive at O'Brien's Bridge, Castle Connell, Plassey
and Corbally and the ESB confirmed that it has to maintain a statutory
compensation flow to the original river and as a result it says frequently there
is little or no generation at Ardna Crossia over the summer months. Now
Clare and Tipperary County Councils have written in opposition to the proposed
pipeline and Limerick City and County Council is holding a special meeting
next week to discuss Ishqa Éireann's application and to decide whether or not
it'll make a submission ahead of the deadline for councils which is at the
end of March. You also spoke to anglers Petula and they're concerned about the
impact on fish population. That's right the Lough Derg Anglers Association also
objects to the pipeline. The group represents 14 fishing clubs along the
river and its submission on the plan is supported by 1,500 members. I spoke to
the association's chairman Christopher O'Mara from Ballina and Tipperary and he
said the extraction point of the proposed pipeline is located at the last
holding area for migratory fish before they enter the river and continue
upstream into Lough Derg and they're concerned about the impact on trout and
salmon and I also spoke to Councillor Tony O'Brien in Killaloo County Clare
who insisted that this isn't a case of us versus them. He doesn't like that
characterisation as if people in the Midwest would deny people in Dublin
water. He says everybody in the country is entitled to a clean supply of fresh
water but again made the point that alternatives to the pipeline have not
been adequately explored by Ishqa Éireann. What happens next now Petula?
Well a public consultation on the plan closes today. Local authorities have
until March 30th to make any submissions and Comisión Planola is required to
decide on the matter within 48 weeks and if planning permission is granted
Ishqa Éireann proposes to start construction in 2028 and complete it
within five years. Petula Martin our Midwest correspondent
thank you for that. It is 7.23. Patients with Friedrich's ataxia met with the
Minister for Health in Leinster House yesterday. They're calling for the first
treatment for the condition to be approved on the Irish market. Friedrich's
ataxia is a rare degenerative neuromuscular disease. It affects around
200 people in Ireland. Our reporter Róisín Collins spoke to one of the
campaigners at her home in County Kilkenny. Why is my life being reduced to a number on a spreadsheet?
Emily Felix is a 28 year old trainee solicitor. She is one of only 200 people
in Ireland with Friedrich's ataxia, a degenerative neuromuscular disease. They
are campaigning for a drug called Skyclaris which they say slows the
condition's progression. This drug will give me more years where I can speak
clearly, more years where I can continue working and more years where I can
live independently and also more time to pursue my ambitions including becoming a
solicitor. It's the difference between just surviving the years living with
Friedrich's and actually living them. Without the drug my condition will
progress and it will progress rapidly and my life just would not be worth living.
28 year old Emily has made the difficult decision to use a voice bank to preserve
her voice for the future. I realise that it's not for me, it's for my family and
it's for my family to still have peace of me when I can no longer speak, speak
like myself. Professor Michael Bowery from the National Centre for Pharmaco
economics accepts the benefits of the drug but says cost is a major issue.
We're very clear that this is not a cure but it does improve patients'
outcome. This is a very very expensive medication at approximately 280,000
euro per patient per year. It would require a very large price reduction of
the order of 90% to render it cost-effective. So we have an issue here
in the sense that the drug does improve things but it costs a lot of money and
it's not value for money. Neurologist Dr. Richard Walsh called the drug an
exciting development. This is a childhood onset relentlessly progressive
degenerative disorder which up to now has had absolutely no treatments available
for it. This MOXIE trial and its extension would appear to suggest that
this drug has the potential to slow down the year-on-year progression in patients
treated by about 50%. Although the numbers involved in the scales used would
appear to be small when comparing treated and untreated groups, these
numbers could represent a difference for someone being able to feed themselves,
sit up independently in a chair and communicate clearly with their
families where otherwise they would lose that ability and that's enormous.
The Department of Health said HSE decisions are made on objective, scientific and
economic grounds and Dr. Barry said a final decision on Skyclaris has not yet
been made. Because our recommendation goes to the HSE drugs group who then
make a recommendation to the HSE leadership team and it's the HSE
leadership team that makes the final decision on the reimbursement of this
drug. Families like Emily's say they will continue to campaign for the
drug. She says the NCPE decision shows a deeper societal problem. I think the
government sees people with disabilities as less able to contribute and
participate in society. I would ask the Minister for Health to please believe
that our lives are worth saving. That report from Roisin Cullen, 27 minutes

lot of detail under that. I suppose a few parts of it kind of linked to that is that,

People also told you, this was probably no surprise, that they're worried about what

about their own future. And this is two main areas there, as you say. One, uncertainty

And I suppose one of the evidence then would suggest, in terms of a recommendation, that

not even in school, but it's fascinating and really it's a huge boost

and then back on the machine for maybe 20 minutes. It's not excessive.

It just seemed awesome and it's kind of an accidental
world indoor rowing champion. Very accidental.
Well, I hope they're helping you to fuel all this because rowing can make you very hungry.

And my trainer was horrified to hear I'd fished in chips as well.
That's all good. Mary, good luck on Saturday. Wish you all the best.
